questions.q: Per this lesson, is escalating during an incident generally a sign of failure?
options: No — not escalating when it's warranted is the actual failure
Yes, a DBA should always resolve every incident alone
Only if it happens more than once per month
Yes, escalation always means the DBA made a mistake
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames escalating early on a genuinely large incident as low-cost and appropriate, while escalating too late is the real problem.

questions.q: According to this lesson, who should a DBA escalate to when a problem is rooted in how the application is using the database, not the database itself?
options: The application team, since they own the fix even if the DBA can stabilize the symptom
Management, regardless of the technical nature of the issue
No one — the DBA should always fix application-caused issues alone
SQL Server Support exclusively
questions.explain: A pathological query pattern from a new app deployment is an application-side problem the DBA can stabilize but the app team must actually fix.

questions.q: Why should management be told about an incident with real business impact, even if they can't help technically?
options: Because they're the ones who will field questions about it and need to know regardless
Because management always resolves technical incidents personally
Because Stripe requires notification of all database incidents
Because it triggers an automatic backup
questions.explain: Business-impact incidents get escalated to management for awareness and downstream communication, not necessarily technical help.

questions.q: What three elements make up a good incident status update, per this lesson?
options: Impact (in plain terms), current action, and an ETA only if genuinely known
Root cause, code diff, and server name
A full stack trace, timestamp, and ticket number only
Apology, blame assignment, and next steps for punishment
questions.explain: The lesson specifies impact in non-technical terms, what's being done now, and an honest ETA (or an honest admission that there isn't one yet).

questions.q: Why does the lesson say guessing a specific ETA is risky?
options: Missing a promised time damages trust more than admitting uncertainty and giving a time for the next update instead
SQL Server logs every ETA given during an incident
ETAs are never allowed in a status update under any circumstance
Guessing an ETA always extends the incident's actual duration
questions.explain: False certainty under pressure is a common, avoidable mistake — honest uncertainty with a next-update time is more trustworthy than a wrong guess.
